# Santhavajātaka (Ja 162)

**ID:** Ja 162
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Santhavajātaka* (Ja 162) is a canonical birth story set at Jetavana regarding the feeding of the sacred sacrificial fire (*aggijuhana*), an occasion sharing its background circumstances with the *Naṅguṭṭhajātaka* [Fausböll 1879]. The narrative opens with the canonical verse beginning *Na santhavasmā param atthi pāpiyo* ("Nothing is worse than intimacy [with the wicked]") [Fausböll 1879]. In the story, the Bodhisatta chooses tending the sacred fire in the forest rather than learning the three Vedas and becoming a householder [Bronkhorst 1998]. When he feeds the sacred fire with ghee and milk-rice, the flames flare up and burn down his leaf hut (*paṇṇakuṭi*) [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. Extinguishing the fire with water, he repudiates fire sacrifice, takes up the renouncer path of an ascetic (*isi* / *ṛṣi*), develops spiritual attainments, and at the end of his life reaches the realm of Brahmā [Fausböll 1879; Bronkhorst 1998]. The narrative also reflects on friendship through an observation of a black deer living on intimate terms with natural predators [Anandajoti 2010].
